translation: If [the disease] arises from injury by food, drink, and toil, its external evidence must show at the mouth: one must lose the flavor of grain, the abdomen must be disharmonious, and one must be unwilling to speak. Even if against one's will one makes forced reply, the voice must be timid and weak; there is foaming saliva at the mouth and profuse spittle; clear nasal mucus is sometimes present, sometimes absent — this is the yin pattern. In external contraction of wind-cold, the external evidence must show at the nose: the nasal qi is not free, the voice is heavy, turbid, and not clear, its speech is blocked and stuffy, [yet] vigorous and forceful, and the mouth must be harmonious within. In cold damage, the face is red and the nose is stuffed and dry; in wind damage, at most the nose flows clear mucus [and nothing more]. The Suwen states: "The nose is the visitation of the lung;" the lung qi communicates with Heaven, so in external contraction of wind-cold the nose becomes not free. The mouth is the kuntu [earth]; the spleen qi communicates with the mouth, so in injury by loss of regulation in food and drink and toil, the mouth does not know the flavor of grain, nor does it know the five flavors. It is also said: "[In] injury from food, aversion to food [arises]"— that harm from food is plainly shown.
